stories.head: US drafts plans to use 'mother of all bombs' on Iran, reports say
stories.say: US military planners have reportedly drawn up options to drop America's largest non-nuclear bomb on Iran, but only if President Trump orders the fighting to resume.
stories.stand: Officials say the plans for the MOAB would only be used if President Trump restarts combat, and some doubt it would work on buried sites.
body: US officials have drafted plans to use the Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, known as the MOAB, against targets in Iran, according to CNN and CBS News. The strikes would go ahead only if President Trump orders combat to resume.

CNN, citing US officials, said the possible targets include Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, among them the deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain site. Some officials reportedly doubt the bomb could penetrate deep enough to destroy such facilities.

A White House spokesperson declined to discuss military plans but said the president keeps all options open to stop Iran getting a nuclear weapon. A Pentagon official said it plans for a wide range of scenarios.

The MOAB is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal. It was used once before, in 2017, against an Islamic State cave complex in Afghanistan. The US and Iran have largely held off striking each other in recent weeks, while Iran continues to threaten shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

stories.head: Houthi missiles hit Yemen's presidential palace in Aden, killing five
stories.say: Houthi missiles have struck the presidential palace in Aden, the seat of Yemen's Saudi-backed government, killing five people and injuring sixteen, according to the health minister.
stories.stand: The attack on the al-Maashiq palace marks an escalation in the renewed war between the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces.
body: Houthi missiles struck the al-Maashiq presidential palace in Aden on Thursday. The palace is the seat of Yemen's internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government.

Yemen's health minister said five people were killed and 16 injured. Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the prime minister and cabinet members were safe. Al Jazeera reported that two of the prime minister's bodyguards were among the dead.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had targeted a Saudi military operations headquarters in Aden. That claim has not been independently verified.

The Saudi-led coalition says Houthi attacks on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport this month have killed 17 people. Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces resumed last month after a truce that had held since 2022.

stories.head: Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian oil refineries after brief pause
stories.say: Ukraine has resumed drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, with a fire reported at the Ryazan plant on Thursday. Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Kyiv's three-day pause is over.
stories.stand: Zelenskyy says the pause requested by President Trump is over because Russia kept hitting Ukraine's energy grid; the Kremlin says strikes never stopped.
body: Ukrainian drones hit an oil refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early on Thursday, starting a fire, according to Russian officials. Russia's defence ministry said it shot down 69 drones and four cruise missiles, but debris set the plant alight.

Ukraine had paused refinery strikes for three days after President Trump announced an energy ceasefire on Sunday. Zelenskyy told the Financial Times the pause was over, saying Russia had kept attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Ukraine had never stopped its strikes on Russian energy sites. Russia's deputy prime minister Alexander Novak earlier said refineries in Saratov and Ryazan had been hit.
Russia kept up its own attacks overnight. Ukraine's emergency service said a drone attack on Kirovohrad region killed three people.

stories.head: Three children and an adult killed in Oregon school shooting
stories.say: A teenage gunman has killed three children and an adult at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon. Police say the sixteen-year-old died at the scene, possibly shot by a bystander.
stories.stand: Police say the 16-year-old suspect forced his way into Silver Rail Elementary School on Thursday and was killed at the scene.
body: Three children and one adult were killed in a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday afternoon. Al Jazeera, citing the police chief, said the adult was a teacher.
Police received the first call just before 1pm local time, from a person who said they had been shot at in a car. Minutes later, callers reported a gunman inside the school.
The suspect, aged 16, died at the scene. Police said it was unclear who shot him and that it may have been a bystander. He has not been publicly named.

At least two injured people were taken to St Charles Medical Center. FBI Director Kash Patel said the agency was helping local police. Students were bused to a nearby church to be reunited with families.

stories.head: Commercial goods stop entering Gaza amid dispute over truck fees
stories.say: Israel says no commercial goods are entering Gaza from its side after merchants stopped coordinating over fees allegedly charged by Hamas. Gaza authorities call the claims false.
stories.stand: Israel blames a row between merchants and Hamas over fees; Gaza officials and truckers say Israel is responsible.
body: Israel's COGAT, the military body that oversees humanitarian affairs in Gaza, said on Wednesday that commercial goods had stopped entering the territory. It said Gaza merchants had stopped coordinating shipments with it.

According to COGAT, the merchants objected to a 10,000-shekel (about $3,220) fee that Hamas allegedly charges on each truck, and a demand that 30% of sales be in cash. Gaza's government media office called this disinformation. It said the fee was a voluntary contribution to a fund for widows and orphans.

The head of Gaza's private truckers' union said no commercial trucks from Israel entered on Thursday, and blamed Israeli restrictions. He put total daily truck entries at about 300, two-thirds of them commercial.
Under a US-mediated deal, Israel must allow at least 600 aid trucks a day. Aid groups say merchants supply fresh foods such as fruit and meat, and warn prices could rise ahead of winter.

stories.head: School roof collapse kills dozens of children in Pakistan's Peshawar
stories.say: A school roof has collapsed in the Pakistani city of Peshawar, killing at least twenty-nine people, most of them young children. Police blame a weak, overloaded building.
stories.stand: The roof of a private school fell soon after lessons began on Thursday, and police have arrested the owner.
body: The roof of the privately run Al-Khair Education Center in Peshawar collapsed on Thursday morning, shortly after lessons had begun. At least 29 people were killed, most of them children, along with a teacher.
Peshawar's police chief said the building was structurally weak and that construction work had overloaded the roof. The school owner has been arrested.
Most of the victims were younger than 13. Rescuers and parents searched the rubble for hours, with the narrow street slowing access for emergency teams.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and President Asif Ali Zardari offered condolences. The provincial governor ordered a safety audit of all schools in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

stories.head: Ethiopian forces push into Aksum as Eritrean troops pull back
stories.say: Ethiopian troops and allied fighters have entered the historic Tigray city of Aksum, a conflict monitor says, as Eritrea denies claims its forces suffered heavy losses.
stories.stand: Federal forces have advanced across Tigray this month as tensions with neighbouring Eritrea rise and the US urges de-escalation.
body: Ethiopian government forces and allied Tigray Peace Force fighters have entered the historic city of Aksum, according to the conflict monitor ACLED. Rival Tigrayan fighters withdrew to the surrounding mountains.
ACLED also reported Eritrean troops withdrawing across the border through the town of Zalambessa as Ethiopian forces advanced. Ethiopian forces took Tigray's capital, Mekelle, earlier in October.

A spokesperson for the pro-government militia claimed Eritrean forces had suffered significant casualties. Eritrea's information minister, Yemane Gebremeskel, called the claims false. They could not be independently verified.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged de-escalation in a call with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on Wednesday. Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing armed groups, which Eritrea denies.

stories.head: Ex-DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson jailed for 15 years for child sex abuse
stories.say: Former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson has been jailed for fifteen years at Newry Crown Court for eighteen sex offences, including rape, against two girls between 1985 and 2008.
stories.stand: The former Lagan Valley MP was sentenced at Newry Crown Court for 18 offences against two girls between 1985 and 2008.
body: Jeffrey Donaldson, 63, was jailed for 15 years at Newry Crown Court on Thursday. A jury had convicted him of one count of rape, 13 of indecent assault and four of gross indecency.
The offences were committed against two girls between 1985 and 2008. Police said both victims were seven when the abuse began. Donaldson denied the charges and is appealing his conviction.
Judge Paul Ramsey said Donaldson had doubled down on his denials and shown no remorse. The sentence is 11 years for offences against the first victim and four consecutive years for the second.
His wife Eleanor, 60, was found in a trial of the facts to have aided and abetted the abuse. She cannot be jailed; the judge will later decide between a treatment order and an absolute discharge.

stories.head: Police feared Andrew would cite the King to block searches, papers show
stories.say: Court papers show police feared Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor would block searches of his homes by insisting the King's consent was needed. Both sides now agree the warrants were unlawful.
stories.stand: Newly published High Court documents explain why officers sought warrants for two royal properties, warrants both sides now agree were unlawful.
body: Documents from High Court proceedings show Thames Valley Police feared Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor could obstruct searches by saying officers needed the King's consent, as the homes were on royal land.
Police raided his Sandringham residence and Royal Lodge in Windsor in February. Mr Justice Hilliard said last week both sides had agreed the warrants were unlawful.

Andrew was arrested on 19 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office, over claims he shared sensitive trade envoy material with Jeffrey Epstein. He denies wrongdoing and has not been charged.
Police want to keep the evidence they seized. Andrew opposes this, and a private hearing is due in 2027. His lawyers say police never asked whether he would grant access.

Kaur, an Indian national, is eligible for deportation but no decision has been made. The Home Office said it always seeks to deport foreign criminals at the first opportunity.
Kaur and Digwa are both due at the Court of Appeal on 5 November. The Attorney General argues Digwa's sentence is too lenient.

stories.head: Five people a week died in custody or state care in Scotland last year
stories.say: Two hundred and sixty-one people died in custody or state care in Scotland in 2025, about five a week, researchers say. Deaths after police contact more than doubled, to thirty-four.
stories.stand: A University of Glasgow-led report finds 261 deaths in 2025, with most never publicly investigated and inquiries taking four years on average.
body: The Scottish Centre for Crime and Justice Research recorded 261 deaths in custody or state care in Scotland in 2025. That is up 6.5% on 2024, about five each week.
Most were people detained on mental health grounds (147). There were 51 deaths in prison and 34 after police contact, up from 14 the year before.
The researchers say most deaths get no public investigation. Fatal accident inquiries now take four years on average from death to findings.
Police Scotland said custody safety is its top priority. The Scottish Government said it would consider the research carefully.

stories.head: UK rents hit another record as most regions see monthly falls
stories.say: Average UK rents hit a record one thousand three hundred and eighty-seven pounds a month in September, HomeLet says, up three point three per cent in a year.
stories.stand: HomeLet's index puts the average new tenancy at £1,387 a month, with London rising while eight of 12 regions slipped.
body: The average agreed rent on new UK tenancies reached £1,387 a month in September, according to the HomeLet Rental Index. That is up 0.4% on August and 3.3% on a year earlier.
London drove the rise, with rents up 1.5% in a month to £2,272. Outside London the average fell 0.3% to £1,176, and eight of 12 regions saw monthly falls.
Northern Ireland and the South West had the fastest annual growth, at 5.4%. Wales was the only region where rents were lower than a year ago.
Tenants spend 32.1% of income on rent on average, rising to 40% in Northern Ireland and 38% in London, HomeLet said.

stories.stand: Speaking at IMF meetings in Bangkok, the chancellor signalled that support for households and firms facing high energy bills will not be universal.
body: Chancellor John Healey said on Thursday that cost-of-living support in his 28 October Budget will be targeted and temporary. He spoke at the IMF annual meetings in Bangkok.

He described energy costs as punishing and said the Budget would aim to give households and businesses some breathing space. Industry forecasts suggest the energy price cap could rise by up to 20% in January.
Healey twice declined to rule out extra borrowing but said he would meet his fiscal rules. The IMF has urged that any UK support be used sparingly and withdrawn quickly.
The IMF this week raised its UK growth forecast for 2026 to 1.3% from 1%. Official figures showed the economy grew 0.1% in August.

stories.head: Swedish parliament rejects Magdalena Andersson as prime minister
stories.say: Sweden's parliament rejected Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson as prime minister on Thursday, by two hundred and forty-eight votes to ninety-nine. Three more attempts remain.
stories.stand: The first prime ministerial vote since September's election failed as her would-be partners refused to back a Social Democrat-only government.
body: The Riksdag voted down Magdalena Andersson's bid to lead a Social Democrat-only government on Thursday. Only her own party's MPs backed her.
The Left, Green and Centre parties all voted against. Together with the Social Democrats they hold 176 of 349 seats, but disagree over who should sit in cabinet.
Under Sweden's rules a nominee falls if at least 175 MPs vote against. Speaker Andreas Norlén can put forward up to four candidates; if all fail, a new election must be held.
Andersson said it may take several votes to form a government. Ulf Kristersson continues to lead a caretaker administration.

stories.stand: The probe, which follows a search of Omar's home on Monday, examines how she obtained citizenship after arriving as a refugee from Somalia.
body: The Trump administration is investigating Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar with the aim of revoking her citizenship, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing US officials.
Investigators are examining whether her age was misstated on immigration papers. More than a dozen grand jury subpoenas have been issued, including to relatives.
Federal agents searched her home on Monday and reportedly took her phone, computers and passport. Trump said he had nothing to do with the search.

body: Delegates at a meeting of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Versailles voted on Thursday to end the leap second. The practice has kept atomic time in step with Earth's rotation for about 50 years.

stories.head: Spyware delivered through online ads, researchers confirm
stories.say: Canada's Citizen Lab says an Israeli ad firm let spyware makers infect devices through targeted ads, with no click needed. At least forty-five Al Jazeera devices were targeted.
stories.stand: Citizen Lab says an Israeli ad company let mercenary spyware firms infect targeted devices without any click, including at Al Jazeera.
body: The University of Toronto's Citizen Lab says it has the first public confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through targeted online ads. It calls the technique AdFection.

The researchers say Israeli firm Discover-Tech presented itself as an ad company but let spyware vendors, including Candiru, target individuals as ads loaded. At least 45 Al Jazeera devices were targeted in 2024 and 2025.

Between March and June 2026 the firm's ads ran on about 120,000 websites and tens of thousands of apps. Some appeared on networks of bodies such as the IAEA, though an ad alone does not prove infection.
Google and IAB Europe have removed Discover-Tech from their vendor lists. Citizen Lab said it could not attribute the attacks to a government. Discover-Tech did not respond.

body: Tesla unveiled the second-generation Roadster on Thursday at an event at SpaceX's site near Waco, Texas. The car was first shown as a prototype in 2017 and has been repeatedly delayed.
There are three versions: Performance, Thrust, and an invite-only Rocket. The higher trims use cold-gas thrusters, and a fan system creates suction strong enough to hold the car upside down.
Tesla quotes more than 300 miles of range and a top speed above 230mph for the Rocket. In the demonstration the car climbed an inverted ramp and used thrusters to hop over other vehicles.
Reservations reopened at $50,000, with $5,000 due upfront. The Thrust package costs $250,000 in total. No base price was given. Musk said production would start in 2028.

body: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is minded to intervene in Sky's proposed £1.6bn takeover of ITV's media and entertainment arm. The deal, agreed in July, covers ITV's free-to-air channels and the ITVX streaming service.
ITV Studios, the production business, is not part of the sale. Sky is owned by the US media group Comcast.

Ms Nandy cited concerns about free expression and the range of views in news media. She also told MPs the deal could affect the availability of varied programming on on-demand platforms, which current merger law does not cover.

stories.head: Bronze Age wreck off Turkey may be world's oldest known shipwreck
stories.say: Jars found off Kekova Island in southern Turkey point to a ship that sank up to four thousand seven hundred years ago. Turkey's culture minister calls it the world's oldest wreck.
stories.stand: Early Bronze Age jars found off Kekova Island in Antalya suggest a ship that sank 4,400 to 4,700 years ago, Turkish officials and researchers say.
body: Turkey's Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy has announced what he called the world's oldest shipwreck, off Kekova Island in Antalya province. It is dated to roughly 4,400 to 4,700 years ago.
No wooden hull survives, so the age is estimated from the style of the amphorae, or storage jars, found on the seabed. The minister says the jars were probably made in workshops in the Jordan Valley.

The work is led by Associate Professor Hakan Öniz of Akdeniz University, with excavation under the Antalya Museum Directorate. A preliminary report was published in July. Small traces of residue remain inside some jars and are still being studied.
